metadata.title: The Boundedness of the (Sub)Bilinear Maximal Function along "non-flat" smooth curves

nodes.name: Bilinear maximal function along the curve $\Gamma$ ($M_\Gamma$)
nodes.statement: That is, given $\Gamma=(t,-\gamma(t))$ where $\gamma$ is a suitable smooth, non-flat curve near zero and near infinity, we ask about the boundedness properties of the bilinear maximal function along $\Gamma$ defined by \begin{align} M_\Gamma&:\s(\R)\times\s(\R)\to L^{\infty}(\R) \nonumber\\ M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)&:=\sup\limits_{\e>0} \frac{1}{2\e} \int_{-\e}^\e |f(x-t)g(x+\gamma(t))|dt. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The bilinear maximal function along $\Gamma=(t,-\gamma(t))$ is the supremum over $\e>0$ of the average of $|f(x-t)g(x+\gamma(t))|$ on $[-\e,\e]$.
differentia: $\gamma$ is a suitable smooth, non-flat curve near zero and near infinity

nodes.name: Bilinear Hilbert transform along $\Gamma$ ($H_\Gamma$)
nodes.statement: The problem regarding the boundedness properties of the maximal bilinear operator $M_{\G}$ and of its singular integral analogue defined by \beq H_{\Gamma}(f,g)(x):= \textrm{p.v.}\int_{\R} f(x-t)\,g(x+\g(t))\frac{dt}{t} \eeq
nodes.statement_short: The singular-integral analogue of $M_\Gamma$, given by the principal-value integral of $f(x-t)g(x+\g(t))\frac{dt}{t}$.

nodes.name: Lacey-Thiele bounds for the bilinear Hilbert transform (flat case)
nodes.statement: This was approached by M. Lacey and C. Thiele in \cite{lt1} and \cite{lt2} where they proved that $H_{\Gamma}$ obeys $L^p\times L^q \to L^r$ bounds\footnote{It is still an open problem if this range is optimal.} for $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{r}$ with $1<p,\,q\leq \infty$ and $\frac{2}{3}<r<\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: In the flat case $\g(t)=at$, $H_\Gamma$ maps $L^p\times L^q\to L^r$ for Holder indices with $\frac{2}{3}<r<\infty$.

nodes.name: Optimality of the Lacey-Thiele range for $H_\Gamma$
nodes.statement: It is still an open problem if this range is optimal.

nodes.name: Lacey's bounds for the bilinear maximal function (flat case)
nodes.statement: The analogous result for the operator $M_{\Gamma}$ was proved by Lacey in \cite{la3}.
conclusions: The analogous result for the operator $M_{\Gamma}$ was proved by Lacey in \cite{la3}.

nodes.name: X. Li's $L^2\times L^2\to L^1$ bound for $H_\Gamma$ along monomials
nodes.statement: in the nonzero-curvature (or non-flat) case, \emph{e.g.} when $\g''$ is nonzero near origin and infinity, the problem of providing bounds for $H_{\Gamma}$ was first addressed by X. Li (\cite{li}), in the special case $\Gamma(t) = (t, t^d)$, $2 \leq d \in \mathbb N$, by proving that $H_{\Gamma}$ obeys $L^{2}\times L^{2} \to L^{1}$ bounds. His proof relies on the concept of $\sigma$-uniformity introduced in \cite{cltt} and is inspired by Gowers's work in \cite{gowers}.
nodes.statement_short: For monomial curves $\Gamma(t)=(t,t^d)$, $H_\Gamma$ is bounded $L^2\times L^2\to L^1$, via $\sigma$-uniformity.
assumptions: in the special case $\Gamma(t) = (t, t^d)$, $2 \leq d \in \mathbb N$

nodes.name: Lie's maximal range for $H_\Gamma$ along curves in $\NF$
nodes.statement: In \cite{lie2015boundedness} and \cite{lie2015triangle} the second author of the present paper proved the maximal range up to end-points for $H_{\G}$ where here $\g$ belongs to a suitable class of curves $\n\f$ that includes in particular any generalized (Laurent) real polynomial with no linear term.
nodes.statement_short: For $\g$ in the class $\NF$, $H_\G$ obeys the maximal boundedness range up to endpoints.
assumptions: $\g$ belongs to a suitable class of curves $\n\f$ that includes in particular any generalized (Laurent) real polynomial with no linear term
conclusions: proved the maximal range up to end-points for $H_{\G}$

nodes.name: Li-Xiao uniform estimates for $H_\Gamma$ and $M_\Gamma$ along polynomials
nodes.statement: Later, elaborating on the ideas and techniques in both \cite{li} and \cite{lie2015boundedness}, the authors in \cite{liXiao2016uniform} prove for both $H_{\Gamma}$ and $M_{\Gamma}$ the expected H\"older range in the case $\g(t)$ a standard polynomial with no linear term with bounds that are uniform in the polynomial's coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: For standard polynomials with no linear term, both $H_\Gamma$ and $M_\Gamma$ obey the Holder range with coefficient-uniform bounds.
assumptions: in the case $\g(t)$ a standard polynomial with no linear term
conclusions: the expected H\"older range in the case $\g(t)$ a standard polynomial with no linear term with bounds that are uniform in the polynomial's coefficients

nodes.name: The class $\NF$ of smooth ``non-flat'' curves
nodes.statement: In what follows, we refer to \cite[Section 2]{lie2015boundedness} for the definition of the class $\NF$ of smooth ``non-flat'' curves near zero and infinity.

nodes.name: Main Theorem: sharp $L^p\times L^q\to L^r$ boundedness of $M_\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(t,-\gamma(t))$ be a curve such that\footnote{It is easy to notice that our main result extends to the class of curves $\NF^{C}$ that is defined to be the set of all curves $\g\,+\,C$ with $\g\in\NF$ and $C\in\R$, \textit{i.e.}, our result is closed under translation by constants of $\g$ with $\g\in\NF$.} $\gamma\in\NF$. Consider the bilinear maximal function defined by \eqref{definition}. Then $M_\Gamma$ extends boundedly from $L^p(\R)\times L^{q}(\R)$ into $L^r(\R)$ where the indices $p, q, r$ obey \begin{equation} \frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{r}, \end{equation} and\footnote{Observe that one gets trivially the desired bound for the triple of indices $(p,q,r)=(\infty,\infty,\infty)$ corresponding to the point $C$ in Figure \ref{triangle_fig}. That is why we will exclude this case from all our future reasonings.} \begin{equation} 1<p\leq\infty\,,\, 1<q\leq\infty \mbox{ and } 1\leq r\leq \infty. \end{equation} This result is sharp.
nodes.statement_short: For $\gamma\in\NF$, $M_\Gamma$ is bounded $L^p\times L^q\to L^r$ on the whole Holder range $1<p,q\le\infty$, $1\le r\le\infty$, and this is sharp.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(t,-\gamma(t))$ be a curve such that
conclusions: Then $M_\Gamma$ extends boundedly from $L^p(\R)\times L^{q}(\R)$ into $L^r(\R)$

nodes.name: Hölder relation between the indices $p,q,r$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{r}, \end{equation}

nodes.name: Admissible range of the indices $p,q,r$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} 1<p\leq\infty\,,\, 1<q\leq\infty \mbox{ and } 1\leq r\leq \infty. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Optimality of the range: necessity of $r\ge1$ for $\gamma\in\NF$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}_d$ be the class of all real polynomials of degree $d$ with no linear and constant terms. In \cite[Section 3]{liXiao2016uniform}, the authors show that for any $d\in\N$, $d\ge2$, there exists a polynomial $P_d\in\mathcal{P}_d$ such that for $\Gamma=(t,P(t))$ one has that $M_\Gamma$ is unbounded whenever $p, q, r$ obey \eqref{exponents10} with $1<p, q<\infty$ and $r<\frac{d-1}{d}$. However, for any $d\in\N$, $d\ge2$ we have that $\mathcal{P}_d\subset\NF$. Thus, in order for \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20} to hold for any $\gamma\in\NF$ we must have $r\ge 1$, hence the claimed optimality of the range in our theorem above.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\mathcal{P}_d\subset\NF$ and Li-Xiao exhibit polynomials with $M_\Gamma$ unbounded for $r<\frac{d-1}{d}$, the range for $\gamma\in\NF$ forces $r\ge1$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{P}_d$ be the class of all real polynomials of degree $d$ with no linear and constant terms
conclusions: in order for \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20} to hold for any $\gamma\in\NF$ we must have $r\ge 1$

nodes.name: Dyadic decomposition of $H_\G$ into pieces $H_j$ with mean-zero kernels
nodes.statement: The bilinear Hilbert transform $H_{\G}$ can be written as \begin{equation} H_{\G}(f,g)=\sum_{j\in\Z} H_j(f,g):=\sum_{j\in\Z} \int_{\R} f(x-t)\,g(x+\g(t)) \r_j(t)\,dt\,, \end{equation} where here $\rho_j(t)=2^j\,\rho(2^j t)$ for a suitable $\rho\in C^\infty_0(\R)$ with $\supp \rho \subseteq\{t\in\R|\frac{1}{4}<|t|<1\}$ and obeying the \emph{mean zero condition} \begin{equation} \int_{\R}\rho(t)dt=0\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $H_\G=\sum_j H_j$ with kernels $\r_j(t)=2^j\r(2^jt)$ supported in $\frac14<|t|<1$ and satisfying the mean-zero condition.
nodes.genus: pieces of the bilinear Hilbert transform
differentia: $\rho_j(t)=2^j\,\rho(2^j t)$ for a suitable $\rho\in C^\infty_0(\R)$ with $\supp \rho \subseteq\{t\in\R|\frac{1}{4}<|t|<1\}$

nodes.name: Dyadic decomposition of $M_\G$ into pieces $M_j$ with kernels integrating to one
nodes.statement: In contrast with this, assuming from now on wlog that $f,\,g\geq 0$, the bilinear maximal function $M_{\G}$ can be expressed as \begin{equation} M_{\G}(f,g)=\sup_{j\in\Z} M_j(f,g):=\sup_{j\in\Z} \int_{\R} f(x-t)\,g(x+\g(t))\underline{\r}_j(t)\,dt\,, \end{equation} where as before $\underline{\rho}_j(t)=2^j\,\underline{\rho}(2^j t)$ for a suitable $\underline{\rho}\in C^\infty_0(\R)$ \emph{positive} with $\supp \underline{\rho} \subseteq\{t\in\R|\frac{1}{4}<|t|<1\}$ and obeying \begin{equation} \int_{\R}\underline{\rho}(t)dt=1\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $M_\G=\sup_j M_j$ with positive kernels $\underline{\r}_j(t)=2^j\underline{\r}(2^jt)$ supported in $\frac14<|t|<1$ and integrating to one.
nodes.genus: pieces of the bilinear maximal function
differentia: $\underline{\rho}_j(t)=2^j\,\underline{\rho}(2^j t)$ for a suitable $\underline{\rho}\in C^\infty_0(\R)$ \emph{positive} with $\supp \underline{\rho} \subseteq\{t\in\R|\frac{1}{4}<|t|<1\}$

nodes.name: Remark 1: $l^1$-sum with mean zero versus $l^\infty$-sum with mass one
nodes.statement: \noindent \textsf{Remark 1} \emph{Thus, in a nutshell, one has \begin{itemize} \item $H_{\G}$ is a conditional $l^1$-sum of pieces $\{H_j\}_{j\in\Z}$ with the associated kernels $\{\r_j\}$ having mean zero; \item $M_{\G}$ is an $l^{\infty}$-sum of pieces $\{M_j\}_{j\in\Z}$ with the associated kernels $\{\underline{\r}_j\}$ integrating to one. \end{itemize}}
nodes.statement_short: $H_\G$ is a conditional $l^1$-sum of mean-zero pieces while $M_\G$ is an $l^\infty$-sum of pieces whose kernels integrate to one.

nodes.name: Three-component decomposition $M_j=M_j^L+M_j^{H\not\Delta}+M_j^{H\Delta}$
nodes.statement: Once at this point, one can isolate the corresponding components $M_j$ (and $H_j$) and regard them as bilinear Fourier multiplier operators. In doing so, it becomes transparent that the phase oscillation in the integral definition of the multiplier will play a key role in the proof. Thus, following the strategy designed for $H_{\G}$ in \cite{lie2015boundedness}, we analyze the stationary points of the phase and decompose accordingly\footnote{Same type of decomposition holds for $H_j$.} \begin{equation} M_j=M_j^L+M_j^{H\not\Delta}+M_j^{H\Delta}\,, \end{equation} where \begin{itemize} \item $M_j^L$ is the $j-$low frequency component (essentially no phase oscillation); \item $M_j^{H\not\Delta}$ is the $j-$high frequency component away from the stationary points region; \item $M_j^{H\Delta}$ is the $j-$high frequency component along the stationary points region. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Each piece $M_j$ splits into a low-frequency part, a high-frequency part away from the stationary points, and a high-frequency part along them.
differentia: $M_j^L$ is the $j-$low frequency component (essentially no phase oscillation)
$M_j^{H\not\Delta}$ is the $j-$high frequency component away from the stationary points region
$M_j^{H\Delta}$ is the $j-$high frequency component along the stationary points region

nodes.name: Remark 2: only the low-frequency components feel the mean-zero/mass-one distinction
nodes.statement_short: Only $M_j^L$ and $H_j^L$ are sensitive to mean zero versus mass one, so the two high-frequency components of $M_j$ and $H_j$ may be identified.

nodes.name: Strategy for the three components of $\M_\Gamma$
nodes.statement:
From here on, the strategy follows the dichotomy present in \cite{lie2015boundedness}, \cite{lie2015triangle} and \cite{lie2019unifiedap}:  egin{itemize} \item the control over the low frequency component $\M^L_\Gamma:=\sup_j |M_j^L|$ is obtained via Taylor series expansions exploiting the lack of oscillation on the multiplier side; indeed, Theorem ef{low_frequency_theorem} states that ootnote{Here $M$ stands for the standard Hardy-Littlewood maximal function.}  egin{equation} |\M_\Gamma^L(f,g)(x)|\lesssim_\gamma Mf(x)Mg(x). \end{equation} \item the bounds for the high frequency component away from the stationary points region $\M^{H
ot\Delta}_\Gamma:=\sup_{j} |M_j^{H
ot\Delta}|$ rely on a further discretization combined with (non)-stationary principle in disguise - essentially a careful integration by parts procedure - and a novel shifted square/maximal function argument. As a byproduct of the latter, each of the elementary building blocks in the decomposition of $\M^{H
ot\Delta}_\Gamma$ will be pointwise bounded by a product of shifted maximal functions (multiplied by a suitable decaying factor) thus mirroring \eqref{lf} (see relation \eqref{mvst}). The superposition of these pointwise estimates will provide us with the global control over $\M^{H
ot\Delta}_\Gamma$. This is the content of Theorem ef{far_theorem}. \item the high frequency component along the stationary points region defined as $\M^{H\Delta}_\Gamma:=\sup_{j}| M_j^{H\Delta}|$ is of course the main term of our operator. After the linearization of the supremum, one decomposes the main term as  egin{equation} M_{j(x)}^{H\Delta}(f,g)(x)=\sum_{m\in\N} M_{j(x),m}^{H\Delta}(f,g)(x)\,, \end{equation} where each $M_{j(x),m}^{H\Delta}(f,g)(x)$ has the phase of the multiplier oscillating at height $\approx2^m$. Applying now Remark 2, for $j(x)=j$, one can identify $M_{j,m}^{H\Delta}(f,g)$ with the analogue $H_{j,m}^{H\Delta}(f,g)$ and thus use the key estimate obtained in \cite[Theorem 3]{lie2015boundedness} to get that there exists $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ such that, for any $j\in \Z$ and $m\in\N$, one has  egin{equation} \|M^{H\Delta}_{j,m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_{\gamma} 2^{-\epsilon m}\|f\|_2\,\|g\|_{2}. \end{equation} At this point hinted by Remark 1 and the approach in \cite{lie2015boundedness}, one makes the simple observation  egin{equation} \|M^{H\Delta}_{j(x),m}(f,g)(x)\|_{L^1(dx)}\leq \sum_{j} \|M^{H\Delta}_{j,m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_{\gamma} 2^{-\epsilon m}\|f\|_2\,\|g\|_{2}\,, \end{equation} where in the last line we used Cauchy-Schwarz and the almost orthogonality of the inputs along the sequence $\{M^{H\Delta}_{j,m}(f,g)\}_{j\in\Z}$. This takes care of the bound $L^2	imes L^2 	o L^1$. The complete boundedness range, stated in Theorem ef{high_frequency_diagonal theorem} relies in part on the techniques developed in \cite{lie2015triangle} along with (shifted or generalized) square function arguments. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Roadmap: Taylor expansion for $\M^L_\Gamma$, integration by parts plus shifted square/maximal functions for $\M^{H\not\Delta}_\Gamma$, and the transferred key $2^{-\epsilon m}$ decay for the diagonal term.

nodes.name: Non-negativity of the input functions $f,g$
nodes.statement: Without lost of generality, from now on throughout the paper, we will assume that $f$ and $g$ are non-negative functions. For transparency, we will mostly follow the notations and conventions as in \cite{lie2015boundedness}.

nodes.name: Dilation, multiplication and differentiation notation for Schwartz functions
nodes.statement: For example, given any $\phi\in\s(\R)$, $j,\,l\in\Z$ and $k\in\N$, we set \begin{align} \phi_j(x)&:=\phi\big(\frac{x}{2^j}\big),\\ \tilde\phi_{l}(x)&:=x^l\phi(x),\\ \phi^{(k)}(x)&:=\left(\frac{d}{dx}\right)^k\phi(x),\\ \tilde\phi_{l,j}(x)&:=\tilde\phi_l\big(\frac{x}{2^j}\big). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Notation: $\phi_j$ is the $2^j$-dilate, $\tilde\phi_l(x)=x^l\phi(x)$, $\phi^{(k)}$ the $k$-th derivative, and $\tilde\phi_{l,j}$ the dilated version of $\tilde\phi_l$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform and inverse Fourier transform
nodes.statement: If $f\in \s(\R)$ we denote the Fourier transform of $f$ with $\hat{f}$, where\footnote{In our later reasonings we will often ignore the constant $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$.} $$\hat{f}(\xi):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\R} f(x)\,e^{-i x \xi}\,d x\,,\:\:\:\:\:\:\xi\in\R\,$$ and the inverse Fourier transform of $f$ with $\check{f}$, where $$\check{f}(\xi):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\R} f(x)\,e^{i x \xi}\,d x\,,\:\:\:\:\:\:\xi\in\R\,.$$

nodes.name: Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator $M$
nodes.statement: We denote by $M$ the standard Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator defined on $L^1_\text{loc}(\R)$ as \[Mf(x):=\sup\limits_{\substack{I\ni x\\ I\text{ interval}}}\frac{1}{|I|}\int_I |f(x)|dx.\]

nodes.name: $t$-shifted square function $S_t^{\v}$
nodes.statement: For $t\in\R$ and $\v\in C^\infty_0$ with $\v(0)=0$ we define the $t$-\emph{shifted square functions} with respect to $\v$ by \begin{equation} S_t^{\v}f(x):=\Big(\sum\limits_{j\in\Z}\Big|(f* (2^j\check{\v}(2^j\cdot)))\big(x-\frac{t}{2^j} \big)\Big|^2\Big)^\frac{1}{2}\,, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The $\ell^2$ square function of Littlewood-Paley pieces of $f$ evaluated at the shifted points $x-t2^{-j}$.

nodes.name: $t$-shifted maximal function $M^{(t)}$
nodes.statement: and the $t$-\emph{shifted maximal function} by\footnote{As expected, in the maximal function case, the mean zero condition of $\v$ becomes irrelevant and one can replace the original conditions imposed on $\v$ by merely $\check{\v}\in \s(\R)$ any (normalized) function with $\check{\v}\geq 0$ and $\|\check{\v}\|_{L^1(\R)}=1$. Given this, in what follows we no longer specify the dependence of our maximal function on $\v$.} \begin{equation} M^{(t)}f(x):=\sup\limits_{j\in\Z}\Big|(f* (2^j\check{\v}(2^j\cdot)))\big(x-\frac{t}{2^j} \big)\Big|\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The supremum over scales of Littlewood-Paley pieces of $f$ evaluated at the shifted points $x-t2^{-j}$.

nodes.name: $(n,\g_t)$-shifted square function $S_{n,\g_t}^{\v}$
nodes.statement: If $\frac{1}{4} <|t|<1$, $\v\in C^\infty_0$ with $\v(0)=0$, $n\in\Z $ and $\g\in\NF$ we define the $(n,\g_t)$-\emph{shifted square functions} with respect to $\v$ by \begin{equation} S_{n,\g_t}^{\v}f(x):=\Big(\sum\limits_{j\in\Z}\Big|\Big(f*\big\{\frac{1}{\tfrac{2^{-j}\gamma'(2^{-j})}{2^n}} \check{\v} (\frac{\cdot}{\tfrac{2^{-j}\gamma'(2^{-j})}{2^n}})\big\}\Big) (x+\gamma(2^{-j}t))\Big|^2\Big)^\frac{1}{2}\,, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Curve-adapted shifted square function: scales normalized by $2^{-j}\gamma'(2^{-j})/2^n$ and evaluation shifted along the curve to $x+\gamma(2^{-j}t)$.

nodes.name: $(n,\g_t)$-shifted maximal function $M^{(2^n)}_{\g_t}$
nodes.statement: and the $(n,\g_t)$-\emph{shifted maximal function} by \begin{equation} M^{(2^n)}_{\g_t}f(x):=\sup\limits_{j\in\Z}\Big|\Big(f*\big\{\frac{1}{\tfrac{2^{-j}\gamma'(2^{-j})}{2^n}} \check{\v} (\frac{\cdot}{\tfrac{2^{-j}\gamma'(2^{-j})}{2^n}})\big\}\Big) (x+\gamma(2^{-j}t))\Big|\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Curve-adapted shifted maximal function: supremum over scales normalized by $2^{-j}\gamma'(2^{-j})/2^n$, evaluated at $x+\gamma(2^{-j}t)$.

nodes.name: The exponent $p^*$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper $p^*=\min\{p,p'\}$ where $p'$ denotes de H\"older conjugate of $p$.

nodes.name: Positive part $a_+$
nodes.statement: Also we set $a_+:=\max\{a,0\}$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic notation $\lesssim$, $\approx$, $\lesssim_d$
nodes.statement: For $A, B>0$, we say that $A\lesssim B$ if there is $C>0$ such that $A\le CB$. We say that $A\approx B$ if $A\lesssim B$ and $B\lesssim A$. Finally, if $d$ is a real parameter, we write $A\lesssim_d B$ if there exists $C=C(d)>0$ such that $A\le CB$ with the obvious correspondence for $A\approx_d B$.
differentia: we say that $A\lesssim B$ if there is $C>0$ such that $A\le CB$
We say that $A\approx B$ if $A\lesssim B$ and $B\lesssim A$

nodes.name: Dyadic discretization of $M_\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Focusing now on the main subject, we record the following simple observation: since we deal with a positive integral operator, it is enough to study our maximal function with the supremum ranging over dyadic numbers, \textit{i.e.}, letting $\e\sim 2^{j+1}$ with $j\in\Z$, we have that \begin{equation} M_{\Gamma}(f,g)(x)\approx\sup\limits_{j\in\Z}\frac{1}{2^{j+1}}\int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} f(x-t)\,g(x+\gamma(t))\,dt. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Since the operator is positive, the supremum may be restricted to dyadic $\e\sim2^{j+1}$.
assumptions: since we deal with a positive integral operator

nodes.name: Threshold $j_0$: non-degeneracy of $\gamma,\gamma',\gamma''$ near $0$ and $\infty$
nodes.statement: Based on the properties of the curves $\g\in\NF$ we have that\footnote{The condition discussed below will be needed when discussing the boundedness of our operator $M_{\Gamma}(f,g)$ in the regime $L^{\infty}\times L^q$ for $1<q\leq \infty$ - see Subsection 5.2.} \begin{align} \exists\:\:\textrm{(possibly large)}&\:\: j_0\in\N\:\:\textrm{depending only on}\:\g\:\textrm{such that} \\ \textrm{for any nonzero}&\:|t|\leq 2^{-j_0}\:\textrm{or}\:|t|\geq 2^{j_0}\:\textrm{one has}\nonumber\\ |\g(t)|>0,\:\: &|\g'(t)|>0,\:\:\textrm{and}\:\:|\g''(t)|>0\:. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: There is $j_0\in\N$ depending only on $\g$ such that $|\g|,|\g'|,|\g''|>0$ for $0<|t|\le2^{-j_0}$ or $|t|\ge2^{j_0}$.
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: Splitting of $M_\Gamma$ into the scales $|j|>j_0$ and $|j|\le j_0$
nodes.statement: With this, based on \eqref{discretization}, we notice that \begin{align} M_{\Gamma}(f,g)(x)&\lesssim \sup\limits_{|j|>j_0}\frac{1}{2^{j+1}}\int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} f(x-t)\,g(x+\gamma(t))\,dt\,\\ &+\,\sum_{|j|\leq j_0}\frac{1}{2^{j+1}}\int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} f(x-t)\,g(x+\gamma(t))\,dt\,. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $M_\Gamma$ is dominated by the supremum over $|j|>j_0$ plus the finite sum over $|j|\le j_0$.
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: Trivial bound for the finitely many scales $|j|\le j_0$
nodes.statement: Now for the latter term, using triangle and Minkowski's inequality, we trivially have \begin{align*} &\:\:\:\:\left\|\sum_{|j|\leq j_0} \frac{1}{2^{j+1}} \int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} f(x-t)\,g(x+\gamma(t))\,dt\right\|_{L^r(dx)}\\ &\leq \sum_{|j|\leq j_0} \int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} \|f(x-t)\,g(x+\gamma(t))\|_{L^r(dx)}\,\frac{dt}{2^{j+1}}\\ &\lesssim_{p,r} \,j_0\,\|f\|_p\,\|g\|_{q}\,, \end{align*} with $p,\,q,\,r$ satisfying \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20}.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle and Minkowski inequalities bound the $|j|\le j_0$ part by $j_0\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$.
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: Reduction to the scales $|j|>j_0$
nodes.statement: Thus, with a slight notational abuse, we will assume from now on that \begin{equation} M_{\Gamma}(f,g)(x)=\sup\limits_{{j\in\Z}\atop{|j|>j_0}}\frac{1}{2^{j+1}}\int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} f(x-t)\,g(x+\gamma(t))\,dt. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: From now on $M_\Gamma$ is taken to be the dyadic supremum restricted to $|j|>j_0$.

nodes.name: The bump $\underline{\rho}$ and its dilates $\underline{\rho}_j$
nodes.statement: Let now $\underline{\rho}$ be a nonnegative, even, $C^\infty_0(\R)$ function with $\supp \underline{\rho} \subseteq\{t\in\R|\frac{1}{4}<|t|<1\}$ and \begin{equation} \int\underline{\rho}(t)dt=1\,. \end{equation} Set $\underline{\rho}_j(t)=2^j\underline{\rho}(2^j t)$ (with $j\in\Z$).
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: The smoothed dyadic bilinear maximal operator $\M_{\Gamma}$
nodes.statement: With this, standard reasonings show that $M_{\Gamma}\approx \M_{\Gamma}$, where here \begin{equation} \M_{\Gamma}(f,g)(x):=\sup\limits_{{j\in\Z}\atop{|j|>j_0}}\M_{\Gamma,j}(f,g)(x):=\sup\limits_{{j\in\Z}\atop{|j|>j_0}}\int_\R f(x-t)g(x+\gamma(t))\underline{\rho}_j(t)dt\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\M_\Gamma$ replaces the sharp cut-off average by convolution against $\underline{\rho}_j$, and satisfies $M_\Gamma\approx\M_\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: Fourier-side (multiplier) representation of $\M_\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Turning our attention on the Fourier side, we have that \begin{equation} \M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)=\sup\limits_{{j\in\Z}\atop{|j|>j_0}} \int_\R\int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)m_j(\xi,\eta)e^{i\xi x}e^{i\eta x}d\xi d\eta\,, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\M_\Gamma$ is a supremum over $j$ of bilinear Fourier multiplier operators with symbols $m_j$.
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: The multiplier $m_j(\xi,\eta)$
nodes.statement: where the multiplier is given by \begin{equation} m_j(\xi,\eta):=\int_\R e^{-i\xi t}e^{i\eta \gamma(t)} \underline{\rho}_j(t)dt =\int_\R e^{-i\frac{\xi}{2^j} t}e^{i\eta \gamma(\frac{t}{2^j})} \underline{\rho}(t)dt. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: The phase function $\varphi_{\xi,\eta}$
nodes.statement: Since the integrand in $m_{j}$ is highly oscillatory, the analysis of our multiplier relies fundamentally on understanding the stationary points of the phase function \begin{equation} \varphi_{\xi,\eta}(t):=-\frac{\xi}{2^{j}}t+\eta\gamma\big(\frac{t}{2^{j}}\big)\:. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: The Littlewood-Paley partition of unity $\phi$
nodes.statement: Let now $\phi$ be a positive even Schwartz function supported in $\{t:\frac{1}{2}\le|t|\le 2\}$ with $$\sum_{n\in\Z}\phi_n(t)=1\:\:\: \textrm{for all}\:\:\:t\not=0\,.$$
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: The multiplier pieces $m_{j,m,n}$
nodes.statement: Then, for every $j\in\Z\setminus [-j_0,\,j_0]$, we write \begin{equation} m_j=\sum_{m,n\in\Z} m_{j,m,n}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} m_{j,m,n}(\xi,\eta):=m_j(\xi,\eta)\,\phi(\frac{\xi}{2^{m+j}})\,\phi\Big(\frac{\gamma'(2^{-j})\eta}{2^{n+j}}\Big)\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $m_j$ is split into pieces localizing $\frac{\xi}{2^{m+j}}$ and $\frac{\gamma'(2^{-j})\eta}{2^{n+j}}$ to unit size.
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: Decomposition $m_j=m_j^L+m_j^{H\not\Delta}+m_j^{H\Delta}$ and the diagonal set $\Delta$
nodes.statement: From the stationary phase principle we have that the main contribution for the integrand in $m_j$ comes from the values near the stationary point(s). With this, we follow the approach in \cite{lie2015boundedness}, and split the analysis of our multiplier into three components, corresponding to the behavior of the phase in \eqref{phmultiplier}, as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item[I)] \underline{\emph{Low frequency case}} - the phase function is essentially constant: \begin{equation} m_j^L=\sum_{(m,n)\in(\Z_-)^2} m_{j,m,n}. \end{equation} \item[II)] \underline{\emph{High frequency far from diagonal}} - high oscillation without stationary points: \begin{equation} m_j^{H\not\Delta}=\sum_{(m,n)\in\Z^2\setminus((\Z_-)^2\cup\Delta)}m_{j,m,n}. \end{equation} \item[III)] \underline{\emph{High frequency close to diagonal}} - high oscillation with present stationary points: \begin{equation} m_j^{H\Delta}=\sum_{(m,n)\in\Delta}m_{j,m,n}. \end{equation} \end{enumerate} Here $\Delta=\{(m,n)\in\Z^2:m,n\ge0,|m-n|\le C(\gamma)\}$ with $C(\gamma)\ge 1$ a large constant depending only on $\gamma$. With this, we have \begin{equation} m_j=m_j^L+m_j^{H\not\Delta}+m_j^{H\Delta}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The multiplier splits into low frequency ($m,n<0$), high frequency off the diagonal, and high frequency on the diagonal $\Delta=\{m,n\ge0,\ |m-n|\le C(\gamma)\}$.
differentia: Here $\Delta=\{(m,n)\in\Z^2:m,n\ge0,|m-n|\le C(\gamma)\}$ with $C(\gamma)\ge 1$ a large constant depending only on $\gamma$.
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: Linearization of the supremum via the measurable function $j(x)$
nodes.statement: We end our preliminaries by transforming the maximal nature of our operator via a linearization procedure \begin{equation} \M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)\approx\int_\R\int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)m_{j(x)}(\xi,\eta)e^{i\xi x}e^{i\eta x}d\xi d\eta \end{equation} where $j(x):\R\to\Z\setminus [-j_0,\,j_0]$ is a measurable function who assigns for each point $x\in\R$ a value $j\in \Z\setminus [-j_0,\,j_0]$ for which $\M_{\Gamma,j}(f,g)(x)$ is at least half of the value of $\M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: The supremum in $j$ is linearized by a measurable $j(x)$ realizing at least half of $\M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)$.
differentia: for which $\M_{\Gamma,j}(f,g)(x)$ is at least half of the value of $\M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)$
nodes.section: 3 Preliminaries: The bilinear maximal function as a multiplier operator; Reduction to the main component

nodes.name: Where the singular/maximal dichotomy manifests
nodes.statement: As discussed in \cite{lie2019unifiedap}, the dichotomy between the singular integral behavior and its maximal version manifests precisely in the low frequency case: indeed, this is the only situation that requires the mean zero condition of the kernel $\frac{1}{t}$ in the bilinear Hilbert transform case which translates, after the standard discretization procedure, into a condition of the from \eqref{mzh} as opposed to \eqref{nzh} in the maximal case. Based on this, the bilinear Hilbert transform required similar techniques with those used to prove the Coifman-Meyer theorem in order to obtain the necessary bounds for the corresponding low frequency component (see \cite[Theorem 1]{lie2015boundedness}). In the bilinear maximal function case, our function $\underline{\rho}$ only satisfies $\int\underline{\rho}(t)dt=1$ but the good news is that - recall Remark 1 in Section 1.3. - we only need to control an $l^{\infty}(\Z)$-sum/norm (in $j$) as opposed to a conditional $l^1(\Z)$-sum in the bilinear Hilbert transform case.
nodes.statement_short: The mean-zero condition matters only in the low-frequency regime; for $M_\Gamma$ one only needs an $l^\infty(\Z)$ control instead of a conditional $l^1(\Z)$ sum.

nodes.name: Low-frequency component: pointwise domination by $Mf\,Mg$
nodes.statement: Set \begin{equation} \M^L_\Gamma(f,g)(x):=\int_\R \int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)m_{j(x)}^L(\xi,\eta)e^{i\xi x}e^{i\eta x}d\xi d\eta. \end{equation} Then, the following holds \begin{equation} |\M_\Gamma^L(f,g)(x)|\lesssim_\gamma Mf(x)Mg(x). \end{equation} Furthermore, for any $p, q$ and $r$ satisfying \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20} we have \begin{equation} \|\M_\Gamma^L(f,g)\|_r\lesssim_{\gamma,p,q}\|f\|_p\|g\|_{q}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The low-frequency part of $\M_\Gamma$ is pointwise $\lesssim_\gamma Mf(x)Mg(x)$, hence bounded $L^p\times L^q\to L^r$ on the full range.
assumptions: for any $p, q$ and $r$ satisfying \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20}

nodes.name: Proof of the low-frequency theorem
nodes.statement:
Fix $m,n \in\Z_-$. From the definition of $\phi$ we have that $ ig| rac{\xi}{2^{j(x)}} ig|,  ig| rac{\gamma'(2^{-j(x)})\eta}{2^{j(x)}} ig|\lesssim 1$, and by property (3) as part of the definition of $\NF$ in \cite{lie2015boundedness}, we have \[ \sup\limits_{t\in\supp\underline{ho}}\Big|\eta\gamma\Big( rac{t}{2^{j(x)}} \Big)\Big|<C_\gamma, \] where $C_\gamma$ is a positive constant that is allowed to change from line to line. Recalling now \eqref{M_multiplierr} - \eqref{mjmn}, we develop the phase in \eqref{phmultiplier} in a Taylor series  egin{align} m_{j(x),m,n}(\xi,\eta)&=\Bigg(\int_\R \sum_{k\in\N}  rac{(-i rac{\xi}{2^{j(x)}}t)^k}{k!}\sum_{l\in\N} rac{(i\eta\gamma( rac{t}{2^{j(x)}}))^l}{l\,!}\underline{ho}(t)dt\Bigg)\phi\Big( rac{\xi}{2^{m+j(x)}} \Big)\phi\Big( rac{\gamma'(2^{-j(x)})\eta}{2^{n+j(x)}}\Big)

Set now  egin{equation} \psi(x):=\sum_{m<0}\phi( rac{x}{2^m})\,, \end{equation} and notice that $\psi\in\s(\R)$ since $\psi=1-\sum_{m\ge0}\phi_m.$ Inserting \eqref{taylor-series} in \eqref{low_freq} and recalling \eqref{notation21}, we have  egin{align} m^L_{j(x)}(\xi,\eta)&=\sum_{k,l\ge0}  rac{(-1)^k i^{k+l}}{k!\,l\,!}C_{k,l} \Big( rac{\xi}{2^{j(x)}}\Big)^k\psi\Big( rac{\xi}{2^{j(x)}}\Big) \Big( rac{\gamma'(2^{-j(x)})\eta}{2^{j(x)}}\Big)^l \psi\Big( rac{\gamma'(2^{-j(x)})\eta}{2^{j(x)}}\Big),\ &=\sum_{k,l\ge0}  rac{(-1)^k i^{k+l}}{k!\,l\,!}C_{k,l} \,	ilde\psi_k\Big( rac{\xi}{2^{j(x)}}\Big) 	ilde\psi_l\Big( rac{\gamma'(2^{-j(x)})\eta}{2^{j(x)}}\Big). \end{align} Thus, putting together \eqref{lowTaylor} and \eqref{operator_low_freq} and recalling \eqref{notation22}, we have  egin{align} \M_\Gamma^L(f,g)(x)&=\sum_{k,l\ge0}  rac{(-1)^k i^{k+l}}{k!\,l\,!}C_{k,l} \Big(\int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)	ilde\psi_k\Big( rac{\xi}{2^{j(x)}}\Big)e^{i\xi x}d\xi\Big) \Big(\int_\R \hat{g}(\eta)	ilde\psi_l\Big( rac{\gamma'(2^{-j(x)})\eta}{2^{j(x)}}\Big) e^{i\eta x}d\eta\Big)

onumber \end{align} We can construct the function $\phi$ such that for every $k\in\N$, the function $\check{\psi}^{(k)}$ has an integrable radially decreasing majorant $\Phi_k$ with $\|\Phi_k\|_1\lesssim C^k$ for some constant $C>0$. Thus, using a classical result in \cite{stein1993harmonic}, one has  egin{align} \Big|\Big(f*\Big\{ rac{1}{2^{-j(x)}}\check{\psi}^{(k)}\Big( rac{\cdot}{2^{-j(x)}}\Big)\Big\}\Big)(x)\Big|&\le \sup_{t>0} \Big|\Big(f*\Big\{ rac{1}{t}\check{\psi}^{(k)}\Big( rac{\cdot}{t}\Big)\Big\}\Big)(x)\Big|

umberthis \end{align*} where here we used \eqref{constcont}. Therefore, \eqref{pointwise_maximal} holds. nodes.statement_short: Taylor-expand the non-oscillating phase, sum the resulting series of Littlewood-Paley-type convolutions dominated by $Mf$ and $Mg$, then apply Hölder and the $L^p$ theory of $M$.

Set  egin{equation} \M^{H

nodes.name: Provenance of the two shifted-function lemmas
nodes.statement: We first state two lemmas which will be used in the proof of the above statement. The first lemma contains two items: point i) represents Lemma 4.8 proved in \cite{lie2015triangle} and can be found in the math literature under various modified forms - see \textit{e.g.} \cite{MS} and \cite{stein1993harmonic}. The second point ii) can be proved with similar techniques to those used for i) and relies in a key fashion on the properties of the class of curves $\NF$. The second lemma mirrors the first one and addresses the maximal function analogue. The case of $M^{(2^n t)}$ was also referred to and proved within Proposition 42 in \cite{lie2019unifiedap}.
nodes.statement_short: Item i) is Lemma 4.8 of the Banach-case paper, item ii) is proved by the same techniques using the $\NF$ properties, and the maximal analogue appears as Proposition 42 of the unified-approach paper.

nodes.name: $L^p$ bounds for the shifted square functions $S^{\v}_{2^nt}$ and $S^{\v}_{n,\g_t}$
nodes.statement: Let $\frac{1}{4} <|t|<1$, $\v\in C^\infty_0$ with $\v(0)=0$, $n\in\Z $ and $\g\in\NF$. \noindent i) Recall the definition of $S_t^{\v}$ given by \eqref{shif_max} in the Notation section. Then, for any $1<p<\infty$, one has -- uniformly in $t$ -- that \[ \|S_{2^n t}^{\v}f\|_p\lesssim_{\v,p} (1+n_{+})^{\frac{2}{p^*}-1}\|f\|_p. \] \noindent ii) Similarly, if $S_{n,\g_t}^{\v}$ stands for the shifted square functions defined in \eqref{shif_maxgama} then, for any $1<p<\infty$, one has -- uniformly in $t$ -- that \begin{equation} \|S_{n,\g_t}^{\v}f\|_p\lesssim_{\g,\v,p}(1+n_{+})^{\frac{2}{p^*}-1}\|f\|_p\:. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Both the shifted and the curve-shifted square functions obey $L^p$ bounds with the logarithmic loss $(1+n_+)^{\frac{2}{p^*}-1}$, uniformly in $t$.

nodes.section: 3.2 High frequency term far from diagonal

nodes.name: High-frequency component along the diagonal: full range boundedness
nodes.statement: Set \begin{equation} \M^{H\Delta}(f,g)(x):=\int_\R \int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)m_{j(x)}^{H\Delta}(\xi,\eta)e^{i\xi x}e^{i\eta x}d\xi d\eta. \end{equation} Then for any $p,\,q,\, r$ satisfying \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20} we have \begin{equation} \|\M_\Gamma^{H\Delta}(f,g)\|_r\lesssim_{\gamma,p,q}\|f\|_p\|g\|_{q}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The main (diagonal) component $\M^{H\Delta}_\Gamma$ is bounded $L^p\times L^q\to L^r$ for the whole admissible range of indices.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Reduction to $m=n$ and to $t$-integration over $\R_+$
nodes.statement: We start by noticing that in \eqref{high-close} it is enough to only consider the case $m=n.$ Also, wlog we assume that our $t$-integration encoded in the expression of $m_{j(x)}^{H\Delta}$ is performed over $\R_+$.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Identification of $T_{j,m}$ and $B_{j,m}$ with the operators of [lie2015boundedness]
nodes.statement: Recalling Remark 2 in Section \ref{MIR}, since the mean zero condition in \eqref{mzh} plays no role in the regions where the phase of the multiplier is highly oscillatory, we are justified from now on to identify our operators $T_{j,m}$ and $B_{j,m}$ introduced below with the corresponding ones defined in \cite{lie2015boundedness}. Consequently, one can transfer with no modifications the theorems regarding $T_{j,m}$ and $B_{j,m}$ in \cite{lie2015boundedness} to our current setting.
nodes.statement_short: Since the mean-zero condition is irrelevant where the phase oscillates, the operators $T_{j,m},B_{j,m}$ may be identified with their bilinear-Hilbert-transform counterparts and all theorems about them transfer.
assumptions: since the mean zero condition in \eqref{mzh} plays no role in the regions where the phase of the multiplier is highly oscillatory
conclusions: one can transfer with no modifications the theorems regarding $T_{j,m}$ and $B_{j,m}$ in \cite{lie2015boundedness} to our current setting.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: The main bilinear operator $T(f,g)$
nodes.statement: Using now the notation from \cite[Section 3]{lie2015triangle} and after some elaborate technicalities, one can prove that the study of the operator with multiplier $m_{j(x)}^{H\Delta}$ can be reduced to the study of the bilinear operator $T(f,g)$ defined by \begin{equation} T(f,g)(x):=\sum_{m\in\N}T_{j(x),m}(f,g)(x)\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The study of $m^{H\Delta}_{j(x)}$ reduces to $T(f,g)(x)=\sum_{m\in\N}T_{j(x),m}(f,g)(x)$.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: The pieces $T_{j,m}$ and their stationary-phase multiplier $v_{j,m}$
nodes.statement: Here, for each $j\in\Z$ and $m\in\N$, we define \begin{equation} T_{j,m}(f,g)(x):=\int_\R\int_\R\hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)v_{j,m}(\xi,\eta)e^{i\xi x}e^{i\eta x} d\xi d\eta \end{equation} and \begin{equation} v_{j,m}(\xi,\eta):=2^{-\frac{m}{2}}e^{i\,\varphi_{\xi,\eta}(t_c)} \zeta\Bigg(\frac{\gamma'(2^{-j})\eta}{2^{m+j}}, \frac{\frac{\xi}{2^{m+j}}}{\frac{\gamma'(2^{-j})\eta}{2^{m+j}}}\Bigg) \phi\Big(\frac{\xi}{2^{m+j}}\Big) \phi\Big(\frac{\gamma(2^{-j})\eta}{2^{m+j}}\Big) \end{equation} where we have \begin{itemize} \item the phase of the multiplier - recall \eqref{phmultiplier} - is defined as \begin{equation} \varphi_{\xi,\eta}(t):=-\frac{\xi}{2^j}t+\eta\gamma\big(\frac{t}{2^j}\big). \end{equation} \item For $\xi,\eta$ fixed, $\varphi_{\xi,\eta}$ has a unique critical point $t_c=t_c(j,\xi,\eta) \in [2^{-k(\gamma)},2^{k(\gamma)}]$, where $k(\gamma)\in\N$ depends only on $\gamma$. \item $\zeta:[\frac{1}{10},10]\times[2^{-k(\gamma)},2^{k(\gamma)}]\to\R$ satisfies $\|\zeta\|_{N-3}\lesssim 1$ for some $N\ge7$.\footnote{The regularity index $N$ here can be lowered but we will not detail this fact here.} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $T_{j,m}$ is the bilinear multiplier operator with symbol $v_{j,m}$, obtained from stationary phase: amplitude $2^{-m/2}$, phase $\varphi_{\xi,\eta}(t_c)$ at the unique critical point, and a smooth factor $\zeta$.
differentia: For $\xi,\eta$ fixed, $\varphi_{\xi,\eta}$ has a unique critical point $t_c=t_c(j,\xi,\eta) \in [2^{-k(\gamma)},2^{k(\gamma)}]$, where $k(\gamma)\in\N$ depends only on $\gamma$.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Limiting behaviour of $\gamma'$ at $0$ and at $\infty$
nodes.statement: Also, from the properties of the class $\NF$, wlog we can assume that \begin{equation} \lim\limits_{\substack{t\to0\\ t\not=0}}\gamma'(t)=0\quad \text{ and } \quad \lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\gamma'(t)=\infty. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Wlog $\gamma'(t)\to0$ as $t\to0$ and $\gamma'(t)\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: The renormalized operators $B_{j,m}$
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item For $j>0$ one sets \begin{equation} B_{j,m}(f(\cdot),g(\cdot))(x):=[\gamma'(2^{-j})]^\frac{1}{2}T_{j,m} \Big(f(2^{m+j}\cdot),g\Big(\frac{2^{m+j}}{\gamma'(2^{-j})} \cdot\Big)\Big)\Big(\frac{x\gamma'(2^{-j})}{2^{m+j}}\Big), \end{equation} that is \[ B_{j,m}(f,g)(x)=2^{-\frac{m}{2}}[\gamma'(2^{-j})]^\frac{1}{2} \int_\R \int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)e^{i(\gamma'(2^{-j})\xi+\eta)x}e^{-i 2^m 2^{j}\Psi_{\frac{\eta}{\gamma'(2^{-j})}}(\xi)}\zeta(\eta,\frac{\xi}{\eta})\phi(\xi)\phi(\eta)d\xi d\eta. \] \item For $j\le 0$ one sets \begin{equation} B_{j,m}(f(\cdot),g(\cdot))(x):=[\gamma'(2^{-j})]^{-\frac{1}{2}}T_{j,m} \Big(f(2^{m+j}\cdot),g\Big(\frac{2^{m+j}}{\gamma'(2^{-j})} \cdot\Big)\Big)\Big(\frac{x}{2^{m+j}}\Big), \end{equation} that is \[ B_{j,m}(f,g)(x)=2^{-\frac{m}{2}}[\gamma'(2^{-j})]^{-\frac{1}{2}} \int_\R \int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)e^{i(\xi+\frac{\eta}{\gamma'(2^{-j})})x} e^{-i 2^m 2^{j}\Psi_{\frac{\eta}{\gamma'(2^{-j})}}(\xi)} \zeta(\eta,\frac{\xi}{\eta})\phi(\xi)\phi(\eta)d\xi d\eta. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $B_{j,m}$ is the rescaled/renormalized version of $T_{j,m}$ (different normalizations for $j>0$ and $j\le0$) whose symbol carries the pure curved phase.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Restriction to $j>0$
nodes.statement: In what follows we will assume $j>0$, as the other case $j < 0$ can be treated in a similar way.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: The functions $R$, $R_j$ and the resulting form of the phase $2^j\Psi$
nodes.statement: From the definition of $\gamma\in\NF$ we define for $x\in\R$ \[ R(u):=\int_1^u r(s)ds \quad\text\quad R_{j}(u)=\int_1^u r_{j}(s)ds, \] then \[ 2^{j}\Psi_{\frac{\eta}{\gamma'(2^{-j})}}(\xi)=\eta R(\frac{\xi}{\eta})+\eta R_{j}(\frac{\xi}{\eta}). \]
nodes.statement_short: Setting $R(u)=\int_1^u r$, $R_j(u)=\int_1^u r_j$, the rescaled phase becomes $\eta R(\xi/\eta)+\eta R_j(\xi/\eta)$.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Discarding the error term $R_j$
nodes.statement: From the properties of $\g\in\NF$ we know that $\lim_{|j|\rightarrow\infty} \|R_j\|_{C^N}=0$. Thus, by properly choosing $j_0\in\N$ in \eqref{threshold} (based on the properties of $\g\in\NF$), one can assume wlog that one has the pointwise estimate $|R_j|\leq \frac{1}{C_{\g}}|R|$ for some large $C_{\g}>>1$. Consequently, $R_j$ behaves as an error term relative to $R$, and thus, for notational simplicity, we will discard $R_j$ in what follows.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\|R_j\|_{C^N}\to0$, one may assume $|R_j|\le\frac{1}{C_\g}|R|$ and discard $R_j$ throughout.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: The operator $B_{j,m}$ with the pure curved phase $e^{-i2^m\eta R(\xi/\eta)}$
nodes.statement: Thus, we have \begin{equation} B_{j,m}(f,g)(x):=2^{-\frac{m}{2}}[\gamma'(2^{-j})]^\frac{1}{2} \int_\R \int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)e^{i(\gamma'(2^{-j})\xi+\eta)x}e^{-i 2^m \eta R(\frac{\xi}{\eta})}\zeta(\eta,\frac{\xi}{\eta} )\phi(\xi)\phi(\eta)d\xi d\eta. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: The amplitude $\zeta$ can be replaced by the constant function $1$
nodes.statement: As in \cite[Section 5]{lie2015boundedness}, one can show that the function $\zeta$ above can be replaced by the constant function $1$. This brings a series of simplifications especially when dealing later with the situation $p\not=2$. Instead of following the argument in \cite[Section 5]{lie2015boundedness}, we present here a much simpler approach: the secret lies in changing the perspective and focusing on the function \[ \varrho(\xi,\eta):=\zeta(\eta,\frac{\xi}{\eta})\,. \] Indeed, by doing this, one can perform a double Fourier series development on $\varrho$ and notice that the linear complex exponentials will preserve the curvature of the phase given by $2^m\eta R(\frac{\xi}{\eta})$; in contrast with this, in the original argument focusing on $\zeta(\eta,\frac{\xi}{\eta})$, after the double Fourier series argument one had to work extra in order to deal with expressions of the form $\{\frac{\xi}{\eta}n_2\}_{n_2\in\Z}$. Returning now to the above definition of $ \varrho$ we notice that $\varrho:[\frac{2^{-k(\gamma)}}{10},10\cdot 2^{k(\gamma)}] \times[\frac{1}{10},10] \to\R$ satisfies $\|\varrho\|_{C^{N-3}}\lesssim_\gamma 1$. This last property follows from the fact that both $\xi$ and $\eta$ are away from $0$. We can now assume without loss of generality that $\varrho$ is compactly supported on $[2\pi,4\pi]\times[2\pi,4\pi]$. Regarding now $\varrho$ as a $2\pi$-periodic function on $\R^2$, we represent it as a multiple Fourier series: \[ \varrho(\xi,\eta)=\sum_{n_1,n_2\in\Z}c_{n_1,n_2}e^{i n_1 \xi}e^{i n_2 \eta}. \] From the hypothesis that $\|\varrho\|_{C^{N-3}}\lesssim_\gamma 1$ with $N\geq 7$, we have \begin{equation} |c_{n_1,n_2}|\lesssim_\gamma \frac{1}{(1+|n_1|+|n_2|)^4}. \end{equation} Thus, for $j>0$, it follows that \begin{equation} B_{j,m}(f,g)(x)=\sum_{n_1,n_2\in\Z}c_{n_1,n_2}B_{j,m}^{n_1,n_2}(f,g)(x) \end{equation} with \begin{equation} B_{j,m}^{n_1,n_2}(f,g)(x):=2^{-\frac{m}{2}}[\gamma'(2^{-j})]^\frac{1}{2} \int_\R \int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)e^{i(\gamma'(2^{-j})\xi+\eta)x}e^{-i 2^m \eta R(\frac{\xi}{\eta})}e^{i\xi n_1}e^{i\eta n_2}\phi(\xi)\phi(\eta)d\xi d\eta. \end{equation} At this point we make the following simple observation: $\|B_{j,m}^{0,0}\|_{L^2\times L^2 \to L^1}=\|B_{j,m}^{n_1,n_2}\|_{L^2\times L^2 \to L^1}$ for any $n_1,\,n_2\in \Z$ since the factors $e^{i\xi n_1}$ and $e^{i\eta n_2}$ can be absorbed into the functions $\hat f$ and $\hat g$ in \eqref{BFourier1} without changing their corresponding $L^2$-norms. Consequently, since \eqref{z-coefficients} implies the absolute convergence of the sum $$\sum_{n_1,n_2}|c_{n_1,n_2}|\,\|B_{j,m}^{n_1,n_2}\|_{L^2\times L^2 \to L^1}=\|B_{j,m}^{0,0}\|_{L^2\times L^2 \to L^1}\,\sum_{n_1,n_2}|c_{n_1,n_2}|\,,$$ one realizes that the boundedness of each of $T_{j,m}$ can be thought as equivalent with the corresponding boundedness of $B_{j,m}^{0,0}$. Therefore, for notational simplicity, we redenote $B_{j,m}$ as $B_{j,m}^{0,0}$ and set $T_{j,m}$ as the correspondent operator associated with the newly defined $B_{j,m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expanding $\varrho(\xi,\eta)=\zeta(\eta,\xi/\eta)$ in a double Fourier series with $O((1+|n_1|+|n_2|)^{-4})$ coefficients, all $B^{n_1,n_2}_{j,m}$ share the same $L^2\times L^2\to L^1$ norm, so one may take $\zeta\equiv1$.
conclusions: one realizes that the boundedness of each of $T_{j,m}$ can be thought as equivalent with the corresponding boundedness of $B_{j,m}^{0,0}$
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: The final normalized operator $B_{j,m}$
nodes.statement: Given the observation above, we will only focus our attention on \begin{equation} B_{j,m}(f,g)(x)=2^{-\frac{m}{2}}[\gamma'(2^{-j})]^\frac{1}{2} \int_\R \int_\R \hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\eta)e^{i(\gamma'(2^{-j})\xi+\eta)x} e^{-i 2^m\eta R(\frac{\xi}{\eta})}\phi(\xi)\phi(\eta)d\xi d\eta\,, \end{equation} or equivalently, on the corresponding operator $T_{j,m}$ obtained from $B_{j,m}$ via \eqref{BTtr1} (and \eqref{BTtr2} respectively).
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Equality of the $L^2\times L^2\to L^1$ norms of $B_{j,m}$ and $T_{j,m}$
nodes.statement: Finally, we record the following key relation: \begin{equation} \|B_{j,m}\|_{L^2\times L^2 \to L^1}=\|T_{j,m}\|_{L^2\times L^2 \to L^1}\:. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Philosophy of our proof
nodes.statement: \noindent\underline{\textsf{Philosophy of our proof}} $\newline$ \emph{Inspired by \cite{lie2015triangle}, our intention is to show that even in the variable case, the operator $$T_{j(x),m}\:\:(\textrm{or equivalently}\:\:B_{j(x),m})\,$$ obeys similar decay bounds with $T_{j,m}$ which can be extracted from the corresponding bounds for the $j(x)=j$ constant case. In other words, one can identify a unified approach that deals simultaneously with both the bilinear Hilbert transform and the maximal operator along non-flat curves.}
nodes.statement_short: The aim is to show that the variable operator $T_{j(x),m}$ obeys the same decay bounds as the constant-$j$ operator, unifying the singular and maximal settings.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Maximal boundedness range for the Bilinear Maximal Function $M_\Gamma$ (Figure 1)
nodes.statement: \textbf{Maximal boundedness range for the Bilinear Maximal Function $M_\Gamma$.} Our Main Theorem states that our operator $M_\Gamma:L^p(\R)\times L^q(\R)\to L^{r}(\R)$ is bounded for all triples $(\frac{1}{p},\frac{1}{q},\frac{1}{r'})$ in the region $\overline{\text{int}(\triangle ABC)}\setminus (\{A\}\cup\{B\})$. This result is sharp.
nodes.statement_short: The boundedness region is the closed triangle $\triangle ABC$ minus the two vertices $A$ and $B$.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Main strategy: two parts and their stages
nodes.statement: \noindent\underline{\textsf{Main strategy}} $\newline$ Recall now the definition of our main operator $T(f,g)$ in \eqref{T}. Our proof will be decomposed into two main parts each split in several stages - see Figure \ref{triangle_fig}: $\medskip$ \begin{itemize} \item First part - \underline{boundedness properties of $T$ on $\text{int}(\triangle ABC)\cup (AB)$} - via $m-$decay bounds for $T_{j(x),m}$: \begin{itemize} \item in the first stage we provide $m-$decay bounds for $T_{j(x),m}$ on the edge $(AB)$; \item in the second stage we provide $m-$decay bounds for $T_{j(x),m}$ on the edge $(CD)$; \end{itemize} Then our result holds in $\text{int}(\triangle ABC)$ by applying interpolation. $\medskip$ \item Second part - \underline{boundedness properties of $T$ on $\partial(\triangle ABC)$}: \begin{itemize} \item for this situation, in the first stage we provide bounds on the edge $(AC]$; \item in the second stage we provide bounds on the edge $(BC)$; \item in the third stage we prove the unboundedness of our operator at the remaining vertices $\{A\}$ and $\{B\}$. \end{itemize} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Part one gives $m$-decay bounds on the edges $(AB)$ and $(CD)$ and interpolates into $\text{int}(\triangle ABC)$; part two treats the boundary edges $(AC]$, $(BC)$ and the unboundedness at $A$ and $B$.
nodes.section: 3.3 High frequency term close to diagonal

nodes.name: Key $2^{-\epsilon m}$ decay for $T_{j,m}$ on $L^2\times L^2\to L^1$
nodes.statement: There exists $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ such that, for any $j\in \Z$ and $m\in\N$, one has \begin{equation} \|T_{j,m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_{\gamma} 2^{-\epsilon m}\|f\|_2\,\|g\|_{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For fixed $j$, the $m$-th piece satisfies $\|T_{j,m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_\gamma 2^{-\epsilon m}\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$.

nodes.name: Variable-$j$ analogue of the $2^{-\epsilon m}$ decay
nodes.statement: There exists $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ such that, for any $m\in\N$, one has \begin{equation} \|T_{j(x),m}(f,g)(x)\|_{L^1(dx)}\lesssim_{\gamma} 2^{-\epsilon m}\|f\|_2\,\|g\|_{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The same $2^{-\epsilon m}$ decay holds for the linearized operator $T_{j(x),m}$.

nodes.name: Tame $L^p\times L^{p'}\to L^1$ bounds for $T_{j(x),m}$
nodes.statement: For any $m\in\N$ and \footnote{Throughout this subsection $q=p'$.} $p,\,p'$ satisfying $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p'}=1$ with $1<p<\infty$, one has \begin{equation} \|T_{j(x),m}(f,g)(x)\|_{L^1(dx)}\lesssim_{\gamma,p} m\,\|f\|_p\,\|g\|_{p'}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Off $L^2$, the variable operator obeys the tame bound with linear growth $m$ in place of decay.

nodes.name: The case $r=1$ follows by interpolation and geometric summation in $m$
nodes.statement: Notice now that for the case $r=1$, our Theorem \ref{high_frequency_diagonal theorem} follows from Theorems \ref{smallk20} and \ref{lpsmgr} above via interpolation and geometric summation in the $m-$parameter.
conclusions: our Theorem \ref{high_frequency_diagonal theorem} follows from Theorems \ref{smallk20} and \ref{lpsmgr} above via interpolation and geometric summation in the $m-$parameter.

nodes.name: The $\ell^1$-in-$j$ operator $T_m$
nodes.statement: Before starting our journey, for $m\in\N$, we introduce the following operator: \begin{equation} T_m(f,g)(x):=\sum_{j\in\Z}|T_{j,m}(f,g)(x)|\:. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Domination of the linearized operator by $T_m$
nodes.statement: We observe that one trivially has \begin{equation} |T_{j(x),m}(f,g)(x)|\leq T_m(f,g)(x)\:. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Bounds for $T_m$: $2^{-\epsilon m}$ decay on $L^2\times L^2$ and tame $m$ growth on $L^p\times L^{p'}$
nodes.statement: With the notations in \eqref{T}, \eqref{Tjm} and \eqref{Tm}, the following hold: \begin{enumerate} \item There exists $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ such that \begin{equation} \|T_{m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_{\gamma} 2^{-\epsilon m}\|f\|_2\,\|g\|_{2}. \end{equation} \item For $p,\,p'$ satisfying $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p'}=1$ with $1<p<\infty$, one has \begin{equation} \|T_{m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_{\gamma,p} m\,\|f\|_p\,\|g\|_{p'}. \end{equation} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The $j$-summed operator $T_m$ obeys both the $2^{-\epsilon m}$ decay on $L^2\times L^2\to L^1$ and the tame bound $m\|f\|_p\|g\|_{p'}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the $L^2\times L^2\to L^1$ decay bound for $T_m$
nodes.statement: Using the following standard notation $\phi_{m+j}(\xi):=\phi\Big(\frac{\xi}{2^{m+j}}\Big)$ and $\phi_{\gamma,m,j}(\eta):= \phi\Big(\frac{\gamma'(2^{-j})\eta}{2^{m+j}}\Big)$ we rewrite \eqref{l2c} in Theorem \ref{smallk2} as \begin{equation} \|T_{j,m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_{\gamma} 2^{-\epsilon m}\,\|f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}\|_2\,\|g*\check{\phi}_{\gamma,m,j}\|_{2}. \end{equation} Using this together with \eqref{Tm} we deduce that $$\|T_{m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\leq \sum_{j\in\Z}\|T_{j,m}(f,g)\|_{L^1}\lesssim_{\gamma} 2^{-\epsilon m}\,\sum_{j\in\Z}\|f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}\|_2\,\|g*\check{\phi}_{\gamma,m,j}\|_{2}$$ which, via an application of Cauchy-Schwarz, further gives $$\lesssim 2^{-\epsilon m}\,\left(\sum_{j\in\Z}\|f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}\|_2^2\right)^\frac{1}{2}\, \left(\sum_{j\in\Z}\|g*\check{\phi}_{\gamma,m,j}\|_{2}^2\right)^\frac{1}{2} \lesssim 2^{-\epsilon m}\,\|f\|_2\,\|g\|_2\,,$$ where in the last inequality we used that the supports of the functions $\{\phi_{m+j}\}_{\{j\in\Z\}}$ and respectively $\{\phi_{\gamma,m,j}\}_{\{j\in\Z\}}$ are almost disjoint, with the latter being a direct consequence of the properties of the curve $\gamma$ (see the property ``smoothness, no critical points, variation near $0$ and $\infty$" in the definition of $\NF$ in \cite{lie2015boundedness}).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the fixed-$j$ bound with Littlewood-Paley pieces, sum in $j$, apply Cauchy-Schwarz and use the almost-disjointness of the frequency supports.

nodes.name: Proof of the tame $L^p\times L^{p'}\to L^1$ bound for $T_m$
nodes.statement:
For this point, of fundamental importance is the approach in \cite{lie2015triangle}. Fix $p,\,p'$ as in our hypothesis and take $f\in L^p$ and $g\in L^{p'}$. In the spirit of \cite[Section 3]{lie2015triangle}, for $h\in L^{\infty}$ (we will assume from now on wlog that $\|h\|_{\infty}=1$ and $h$ is positive), we define ootnote{It is important to notice here that as opposed to the similar object defined in \cite{lie2015triangle}, in our context, in definition \eqref{Ljm} below, the operator $T_{j,m}(f,g)$ is taken with \emph{absolute values} thus making $\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)$ a sublinear ``form".} for each $j\in\Z$ and $m\in\N$  egin{equation} \Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h):=\int_\R |T_{j,m}(f,g)(x)|\, h(x)\,dx. \end{equation} For $m\in\N$, we define  egin{equation} \Lambda_m(f,g,h):=\Lambda_m^+(f,g,h)+\Lambda_m^-(f,g,h), \end{equation} where  egin{equation} \Lambda_m^+(f,g,h):=\sum_{j\in\N} \Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)\quad 	ext{ and } \quad \Lambda_m^-(f,g,h):=\sum_{j\in\Z\setminus\N} \Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h). \end{equation} Since our $\Lambda's$ involve absolute values inside the integral expressions, in order to be able to use the techniques in \cite{lie2015triangle}, we will first apply a linearization procedure. Thus, for a suitable sequence of $L^{\infty}-$functions $\{\ep_{j,m}\}$ with the property $|\ep_{j,m}(x)|=1$ a.e $x\in\R$, we will re-write  egin{equation} \Lambda_m^+(f,g,h):=\sum_{j\in\N} \int_{\R} T_{j,m}(f,g)(x)\, \ep_{j,m}(x)\,h(x)\,dx,\, \end{equation} with the obvious correspondence for $\Lambda_m^-(f,g,h)$. Deduce now that \eqref{l2cpp} is in fact equivalent with  egin{equation} \left|\Lambda_m^{\pm}(f,g,h)ight|\lesssim_{\gamma,p} m\,\|f\|_p\,\|g\|_{p'}\,\|h\|_{\infty}. \end{equation} In what follows we will only focus on the $+$ component since the $-$ component can be treated in a similar fashion. We will split our discussion in two sub-cases $
ewline$ 
oindent	extbf{Case 1.} $1<p\leq 2$ $
ewline$ With the notations ootnote{We will only recall here that $\phi_{j,p_0}(\eta):= \phi( rac{\g'(2^{-j})\,\eta}{2^j}-p_0) $ and $\psi_{m,p_0,j}(\xi):= 2^{- rac{m}{2}}\,e^{- i p_0 R( rac{\xi}{2^j\,p_0})}\,\phi( rac{\xi}{2^{m+j}})$ where $j\in\N$ and $p_0\in [2^m,\, 2^{m+1})\cap \N$ with $m\in\N$.} in \cite{lie2015triangle}, following the first part of the argument provided for the proof of Proposition 4.2 in Section 4 of \cite{lie2015triangle}, we have $$|\ll_{m}^{+}(f,g,h)|\lesssim$$ $$\int_{\R}\left( \sum_{j\in\N}|(f*\check{\phi}_{m+j})(y)|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}\: \left( \sum_{j\in\N} \left|M\left(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})\,((\ep_{j,m} h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})|ight)(y)ight|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}\,dy$$ $$\lesssim \left\| \left( \sum_{j\in\N}|f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p}\, \left\|\left( \sum_{j\in\N} \left|M\left(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})\,((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})|ight)ight|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p'}$$ $$\lesssim \|f\|_{p}\,\left\|\left( \sum_{j\in\N}\left(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})\,((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})|ight)^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p'}\:,$$ where for the last relation we used standard Littlewood-Paley theory (for providing bounds on the square function for $f$) and Fefferman-Stein's inequality (\cite{fefferman1971some}) (for the term involving the functions $g$ and $h$). Using now that  egin{equation} ((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})(x)=\int_{\R} (\ep_{j,m}\, h)(x- rac{\g'(2^{-j})}{2^j}\,y)\,\check{\phi}(y)\,e^{i\,p_0\,y}\,dy\:, \end{equation} we deduce that  egin{equation} \sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})|^2\lesssim_{\g} \|h\|_{\infty}^2\,. \end{equation} Thus, applying Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we get  egin{equation} \left(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})\,((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})|ight)^2\lesssim_{\g} \|h\|_{\infty}^2\,\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})|^2\,, \end{equation} from which we deduce that  egin{equation} |\ll_{m}^{+}(f,g,h)|\lesssim_{\g} \|f\|_{p}\, \|h\|_{\infty}\,\left\|\left(\sum_{j\in\N}\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0}|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p'}\:. \end{equation} Finally, since $p'\geq2$, we are allowed to apply Rubio de Francia's inequality (\cite{rubio1985littlewood}):  egin{equation} \left\|\left( \sum_{j\in\N}\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0}|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p'}\lesssim_{\g,p'} \|g\|_{p'}\:. \end{equation} Putting now together \eqref{CS}, \eqref{L}, \eqref{RF} we conclude that \eqref{l2cppg} holds. $
ewline$ 
oindent	extbf{Case 2.} $2<p<\infty$ $
ewline$ In this second case, we follow part of the argument inside the proof of Proposition 4.3 in Section 4 of \cite{lie2015triangle}. Indeed, by applying Cauchy-Schwarz and then H"older's inequality, we have  eq \eeq $$|\ll_{m}^{+}(f,g,h)|\leq$$ $$\sum_{j\in\N}\int_{\R} \,\left(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}*\check{\psi}_{m,p_0,j})(x)|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}	imes \left(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})(x)\,((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})(x)|^{2}ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}\,dx$$ $$\leq\left\|\,\left(\sum_{j\in\N}\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}*\check{\psi}_{m,p_0,j})|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p} \left\|\left(\sum_{j\in\N}\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})\,((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})|^{2}ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p'}\:.$$ Now the content of Proposition 4.4 in \cite{lie2015triangle} is the statement that for $p\geq2$ one has  egin{equation} \left\|\,\left(\sum_{j\in\N}\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}*\check{\psi}_{m,p_0,j}|^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p}\lesssim_{\g,p} m^{ rac{2}{p'}-1}\, \|f\|_{p}\;, \end{equation} while from the Lemma 4.9 in \cite{lie2015triangle} we deduce that  egin{equation} \sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})(x)\,((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})(x)|^{2}\lesssim_{\g} \|h\|_{\infty}^2\, M(g*\check{\phi}_{\g,m,j})^2(x)\:, \end{equation} where here we recall that $\phi_{\g,m,j}(\eta):=\phi( rac{\g'(2^{-j})}{2^{j+m}}\,\eta)\;.$ Inserting \eqref{Cf} and \eqref{claim} in \eqref{key2}, we conclude that  eq \eeq $$|\ll_{m}^{+}(f,g,h)|\leq_{\g,p} m^{ rac{2}{p'}-1}\, \|f\|_{p}\,\|h\|_{\infty}\, \left\|\left(\sum_{j\in\N} M(g*\check{\phi}_{\g,m,j})^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p'}$$ $$\lesssim_{p} m^{ rac{2}{p'}-1}\, \|f\|_{p}\,\|h\|_{\infty}\, \left\|\left(\sum_{j\in\N} (g*\check{\phi}_{\g,m,j})^2ight)^{ rac{1}{2}}ight\|_{p'}\lesssim_{\g,p} m^{ rac{2}{p'}-1}\, \|f\|_{p}\,\|g\|_{p'}\,\|h\|_{\infty}\,,$$ where we made use again of the Fefferman-Stein's inequality (\cite{fefferman1971some}) (for the second inequality) and standard Littlewood-Paley theory (for the third inequality).
nodes.statement_short: Linearize the absolute values into sublinear forms $\Lambda^{\pm}_m$, then split $1<p\le2$ (Littlewood-Paley, Fefferman-Stein, Rubio de Francia) and $2<p<\infty$ (Cauchy-Schwarz, Hölder plus the imported Proposition 4.4 and Lemma 4.9).

nodes.name: The sublinear form $\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)$
nodes.statement: Fix $p,\,p'$ as in our hypothesis and take $f\in L^p$ and $g\in L^{p'}$. In the spirit of \cite[Section 3]{lie2015triangle}, for $h\in L^{\infty}$ (we will assume from now on wlog that $\|h\|_{\infty}=1$ and $h$ is positive), we define\footnote{It is important to notice here that as opposed to the similar object defined in \cite{lie2015triangle}, in our context, in definition \eqref{Ljm} below, the operator $T_{j,m}(f,g)$ is taken with \emph{absolute values} thus making $\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)$ a sublinear ``form".} for each $j\in\Z$ and $m\in\N$ \begin{equation} \Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h):=\int_\R |T_{j,m}(f,g)(x)|\, h(x)\,dx. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pairing of $|T_{j,m}(f,g)|$ against a positive $h\in L^\infty$; absolute values make $\Lambda_{j,m}$ a sublinear form.

nodes.name: The forms $\Lambda_m$, $\Lambda_m^+$ and $\Lambda_m^-$
nodes.statement: For $m\in\N$, we define \begin{equation} \Lambda_m(f,g,h):=\Lambda_m^+(f,g,h)+\Lambda_m^-(f,g,h), \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \Lambda_m^+(f,g,h):=\sum_{j\in\N} \Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)\quad \text{ and } \quad \Lambda_m^-(f,g,h):=\sum_{j\in\Z\setminus\N} \Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Rubio de Francia's inequality
nodes.statement: Finally, since $p'\geq2$, we are allowed to apply Rubio de Francia's inequality (\cite{rubio1985littlewood}): \begin{equation} \left\|\left( \sum_{j\in\N}\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0}|^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right\|_{p'}\lesssim_{\g,p'} \|g\|_{p'}\:. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For $p'\ge2$ the square function over arbitrary disjoint frequency intervals is bounded on $L^{p'}$.

nodes.name: Square-function bound for $f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}*\check{\psi}_{m,p_0,j}$ (Proposition 4.4 of [lie2015triangle])
nodes.statement: Now the content of Proposition 4.4 in \cite{lie2015triangle} is the statement that for $p\geq2$ one has \begin{equation} \left\|\,\left(\sum_{j\in\N}\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}*\check{\psi}_{m,p_0,j}|^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right\|_{p}\lesssim_{\g,p} m^{\frac{2}{p'}-1}\, \|f\|_{p}\;, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For $p\ge2$ the double square function built from $f$ and the curved kernels is bounded by $m^{\frac{2}{p'}-1}\|f\|_p$.

nodes.name: Maximal-function domination of the $p_0$-sum (Lemma 4.9 of [lie2015triangle])
nodes.statement: while from the Lemma 4.9 in \cite{lie2015triangle} we deduce that \begin{equation} \sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})(x)\,((\ep_{j,m}\, h)*\check{\phi}_{j,p_0})(x)|^{2}\lesssim_{\g} \|h\|_{\infty}^2\, M(g*\check{\phi}_{\g,m,j})^2(x)\:, \end{equation} where here we recall that $\phi_{\g,m,j}(\eta):=\phi(\frac{\g'(2^{-j})}{2^{j+m}}\,\eta)\;.$
nodes.statement_short: The $p_0$-sum of products $|(g*\check\phi_{j,p_0})((\ep_{j,m}h)*\check\phi_{j,p_0})|^2$ is dominated by $\|h\|_\infty^2 M(g*\check\phi_{\g,m,j})^2$.

nodes.name: Bounds on the segment $(CD)$: $L^{2r}\times L^{2r}\to L^r$ decay for $T_{j(x),m}$
nodes.statement: Let $1\le r<\infty$. For $m\in\N$, the following holds \begin{equation} \|T_{j(x),m}(f,g)(x)\|_{L^r(dx)}\lesssim_{\gamma,r}(1+m^{1-\frac{1}{r}})\,2^{-\frac{m}{20r}}\,\|f\|_{2r}\,\|g\|_{2r}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For $1\le r<\infty$ the variable operator satisfies $\|T_{j(x),m}\|_{L^r}\lesssim(1+m^{1-1/r})2^{-m/(20r)}\|f\|_{2r}\|g\|_{2r}$.

nodes.name: $L^p\times L^q\to L^r$ decay bounds for the fixed-$j$ pieces $T_{j,m}$
nodes.statement: Let $p, q, r$ be as in \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20}. Then for any $j, m\in\Z$, we have \begin{equation} \|T_{j,m}(f,g)\|_r\lesssim_{\gamma,p,q}(1+m^{1-\frac{2}{p}})\,2^{-\frac{m}{10}(1-\frac{1}{p*})}\,\|f\|_p\,\|g\|_q. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For all admissible $p,q,r$ the fixed-scale piece obeys $\|T_{j,m}\|_r\lesssim(1+m^{1-2/p})2^{-\frac{m}{10}(1-\frac{1}{p^*})}\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$.
assumptions: Let $p, q, r$ be as in \eqref{exponents10} and \eqref{exponents20}.

nodes.name: Proof of the $L^p\times L^q\to L^r$ bounds for $T_{j,m}$
nodes.statement: Using the notation from (\ref{Ljm}) and \cite{lie2015triangle}, we choose $h\in L^{r'}$ such that \[ \Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)= \int_\R T_{j,m}(f,g)(x)h(x)dx. \] Therefore \[ |\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)|\le \int_\R |(f*\check{\phi}_{m+j})(x)\:|M\Bigg(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j, p_0})(\cdot) (h*\check{\phi}_{j, p_0})(\cdot)|\Bigg)(x)\,dx, \] and \[ |\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)|\le \int_\R\Bigg(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(g*\check{\phi}_{j, p_0})(x)(h*\check{\phi}_{j, p_0})(x)|^2\Bigg)^\frac{1}{2} \Bigg(\sum_{p_0=2^m}^{2^{m+1}}|(f*\check{\phi}_{m+j}*\check{\psi}_{m, p_0, j})(x)|^2\Bigg)^\frac{1}{2}dx. \] Hence, by following the second part of the proof of \cite[Proposition 4.2 ]{lie2015triangle} and \cite[Proposition 4.3 ]{lie2015triangle}, we deduce that the results in \cite{lie2015triangle} hold for $\Lambda_{j,m}$. In particular, the analogue of \cite[Theorem 3.3]{lie2015triangle} follows: \begin{proposition} Let $1<p<\infty$. Then the following estimates hold \begin{equation} Edge\:(AC):\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:|\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)|\lesssim_{\gamma,p} (1+m^{1-\frac{2}{p}})2^{-\frac{m}{10}(1-\frac{1}{p*})}\|f\|_p\|g\|_\infty \|h\|_{p'}, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} Edge\:(AB):\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:|\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)|\lesssim_{\gamma,p} (1+m^{1-\frac{2}{p}})2^{-\frac{m}{10}(1-\frac{1}{p*})} \|f\|_p\|g\|_{p'} \|h\|_\infty. \end{equation} \end{proposition} Thus, Proposition \ref{Tjmb} follows from the Proposition \ref{DeltaM} after applying real interpolation.
nodes.statement_short: Dualize with $h\in L^{r'}$, reproduce the two estimates of the Banach-case argument to obtain the edge $(AC)$ and $(AB)$ bounds for $\Lambda_{j,m}$, then real-interpolate.

nodes.name: Edge $(AC)$ and edge $(AB)$ estimates for the form $\Lambda_{j,m}$
nodes.statement: Let $1<p<\infty$. Then the following estimates hold \begin{equation} Edge\:(AC):\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:|\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)|\lesssim_{\gamma,p} (1+m^{1-\frac{2}{p}})2^{-\frac{m}{10}(1-\frac{1}{p*})}\|f\|_p\|g\|_\infty \|h\|_{p'}, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} Edge\:(AB):\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:|\Lambda_{j,m}(f,g,h)|\lesssim_{\gamma,p} (1+m^{1-\frac{2}{p}})2^{-\frac{m}{10}(1-\frac{1}{p*})} \|f\|_p\|g\|_{p'} \|h\|_\infty. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On the two edges the form $\Lambda_{j,m}$ obeys $(1+m^{1-2/p})2^{-\frac{m}{10}(1-\frac{1}{p^*})}$ decay with $L^\infty$ in the second resp. third slot.

nodes.name: Proof of the bounds on the segment $(CD)$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the fixed-$j$ bound in Littlewood-Paley form, dominate the linearized operator by the $\ell^r$ sum, and combine Hölder, a Littlewood-Paley computation and Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.name: The segment $(CD)$ is not needed for the interior of $\triangle ABC$
nodes.statement: In order to prove our main Theorem \ref{high_frequency_diagonal theorem} in the interior of $\triangle ABC$ it is in fact not necessary to pursue the boundedness of our operator along the edge $(CD)$. Indeed, one could apply interpolation between the bounds corresponding to the edges $(AB)$ and $(AC)$ instead, with the latter discussed in the next section. However, we wanted to offer a less expected but more interesting alternative approach to the trivial bounds one gets along the segment $(AC)$. This is especially useful in situations in which one deals with similar type operators but for which one does not have a good control on the edges $(BC)$ and $(AC)$.
nodes.statement_short: Interpolating between the edges $(AB)$ and $(AC)$ would suffice; the $(CD)$ route is offered as a more interesting alternative.

nodes.name: Proof of the bound on the edge $(AC]$
nodes.statement: From the definition \eqref{definition} of $M_\Gamma$ it is trivial to notice that for all $x\in\R$, \begin{align} |M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)|&\le \|g\|_\infty\, \sup_{\e>0}\frac{1}{2\e}\int_{-\e}^\e |f(x-t)|dt\nonumber\\ &\le \|g\|_\infty\, Mf(x). \end{align} Hence, applying the classical results on the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator we get
nodes.statement_short: Pull $\|g\|_\infty$ out of the average to dominate $M_\Gamma(f,g)$ by $\|g\|_\infty Mf$, then quote the $L^p$ theory of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator.
nodes.section: 5.1 Bounds on the edge $(AC]$: $1< p\le \infty$, $r=p$ and $q=\infty$

nodes.name: Boundedness on the edge $(AC]$: $L^p\times L^\infty\to L^p$
nodes.statement: For any $1<p\le \infty$, one has \begin{equation} \|M_\Gamma(f,g)\|_{L^p}\lesssim_p \|f\|_p\,\|g\|_\infty. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5.1 Bounds on the edge $(AC]$: $1< p\le \infty$, $r=p$ and $q=\infty$

nodes.name: Boundedness on the edge $(BC]$: $L^\infty\times L^q\to L^q$
nodes.statement: For any $1<q\le \infty$, one has \begin{equation} \|M_\Gamma(f,g)\|_{L^q}\lesssim_{\g,q} \|f\|_\infty\,\|g\|_q. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5.2 Bounds on the edge $(BC]$: $1< q\le \infty$, $r=q$ and $p=\infty$

nodes.name: The single-function maximal operator along the curve, $M_\gamma$
nodes.statement: where here \begin{equation} M_\gamma\, g(x):=\sup\limits_{{j\in\Z}\atop{|j|>j_0}}\frac{1}{2^{j+1}}\int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} |g(x+\gamma(t))|dt\,. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5.2 Bounds on the edge $(BC]$: $1< q\le \infty$, $r=q$ and $p=\infty$

nodes.name: Reduction of the edge $(BC]$ bound to the maximal operator $M_\gamma$
nodes.statement: From \eqref{discretizationc}, recalling that $\gamma\in\NF$ and our choice of $j_0$ in \eqref{threshold} - \eqref{threshold1}, we notice that for all $x\in\R$, \begin{align} |M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)|&\le \|f\|_\infty\,M_\gamma\, g(x). \end{align} where here \begin{equation} M_\gamma\, g(x):=\sup\limits_{{j\in\Z}\atop{|j|>j_0}}\frac{1}{2^{j+1}}\int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} |g(x+\gamma(t))|dt\,. \end{equation} Thus, Theorem \ref{finfty} follows from the result below
nodes.statement_short: Pull $\|f\|_\infty$ out of the average, leaving the single-function curved maximal operator $M_\gamma g$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Bounds on the edge $(BC]$: $1< q\le \infty$, $r=q$ and $p=\infty$

nodes.name: $L^q$ boundedness of the maximal operator $M_\gamma$ along the curve
nodes.statement: For any $1<q\le \infty$, one has \begin{equation} \|M_\gamma(g)\|_{L^q}\lesssim_{\gamma,q} \|g\|_q. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5.2 Bounds on the edge $(BC]$: $1< q\le \infty$, $r=q$ and $p=\infty$

nodes.name: Proof of the $L^q$ boundedness of $M_\gamma$
nodes.statement: From the properties of $\g$ and the choice of $j_0$ in \eqref{threshold} - \eqref{threshold1}, it is straightforward to check that for any $k\in \Z$ with $|k|>j_0$ and $t\in[2^k,2^{k+1}]$ one has \begin{equation} |\gamma(2^{k})|\approx_{\gamma} 2^{k}|\gamma'(t)|\approx_{\gamma}|\gamma(2^{k+1})|\,. \end{equation} From \eqref{threshold1}, we deduce that $\gamma$ is strictly monotone and invertible over each of the intervals $(-\infty,-2^{j_0})$, $(-2^{-j_0},0)$, $(0,2^{-j_0})$ and $(2^{j_0}, \infty)$. Wlog we consider from now on that our entire discussion takes place relative to $J_0:=(2^{j_0}, \infty)$ and that both $\g'$ and $\g''$ are strictly positive on $J_0$. Thus, for $k\in\Z$ with $k>j_0$, one has \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\int_{2^k}^{2^{k+1}}|g(x+\gamma(t))|dt &=\frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\int_{\gamma([2^k,2^{k+1}])}|g(x+u)|\frac{du}{|\gamma'(\gamma^{-1}(u))|}\\ &\le\frac{1}{2^{k+1}|\gamma'(2^k)|}\int_{\gamma(2^k)}^{\gamma(2^{k+1})}|g(x+u)|du\,. \end{align*} Appealing now to \eqref{gammak1t}, we deduce \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\int_{2^k}^{2^{k+1}}|g(x+\gamma(t))|dt \leq\frac{1}{2^{k+1}|\gamma'(2^k)|}\int_{-|\gamma(2^k)|-|\gamma(2^{k+1})|}^{|\gamma(2^k)|+|\gamma(2^{k+1})|}|g(x-u)|du \lesssim_{\gamma} Mg(x). \end{equation} Analogously, \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\int_{-2^{k+1}}^{-2^k}|g(x+\gamma(t))|dt&\lesssim_{\gamma} Mg(x). \end{align*} Therefore \begin{equation} \sup_{{j\in\Z}\atop{|j|>j_0}}\,\frac{1}{2^{j+1}}\int\limits_{2^j\le|t|\le2^{j+1}} |g(x+\gamma(t))|dt\lesssim_{\gamma} Mg(x). \end{equation} Using now the standard theory on Hardy Littlewood maximal operator we conclude our Theorem \ref{Mgamma}.
nodes.statement_short: On each dyadic block change variables $u=\gamma(t)$ using strict monotonicity of $\gamma$, use $|\gamma(2^k)|\approx2^k|\gamma'(t)|\approx|\gamma(2^{k+1})|$ to dominate by $Mg$, and quote the Hardy-Littlewood theory.
nodes.section: 5.2 Bounds on the edge $(BC]$: $1< q\le \infty$, $r=q$ and $p=\infty$

nodes.name: Unboundedness at the vertex $A$ ($p=r=1$, $q=\infty$)
nodes.statement: We start by focusing on the vertex $A$, \ie, $p=r=1$ and $q=\infty$. In this case, we show that there are functions $f\in L^1(\R)$, $g\in L^\infty(\R)$, and a map $\gamma\in\NF$ such that $M_\Gamma(f,g)$ is not bounded on $L^1$.
nodes.statement_short: There exist $f\in L^1$, $g\in L^\infty$ and $\gamma\in\NF$ with $M_\Gamma(f,g)\notin L^1$.
conclusions: we show that there are functions $f\in L^1(\R)$, $g\in L^\infty(\R)$, and a map $\gamma\in\NF$ such that $M_\Gamma(f,g)$ is not bounded on $L^1$
nodes.section: 5.3 Behavior on $\{A\}\cup\{B\}$: triples $p=r=1,\, q=\infty$ and $p=\infty,\, q=r=1$

nodes.name: Counterexample at the vertex $A$: $f=\chi_{[-1,1]}$, $g=\chi_{(-\infty,1)}$, $\gamma(t)=t^2$
nodes.statement: Let $f=\chi_{[-1,1]}$ and $g=\chi_{(-\infty,1)}$ be characteristic functions, and let $\gamma(t)=t^2\in\NF$. Note that $f\in L^1(\R)$, $g\in L^\infty(\R)$ with $\|f\|_1=2$, and $\|g\|_\infty=1$.
nodes.section: 5.3 Behavior on $\{A\}\cup\{B\}$: triples $p=r=1,\, q=\infty$ and $p=\infty,\, q=r=1$

nodes.name: Proof of the unboundedness at the vertex $A$
nodes.statement: Let $f=\chi_{[-1,1]}$ and $g=\chi_{(-\infty,1)}$ be characteristic functions, and let $\gamma(t)=t^2\in\NF$. Note that $f\in L^1(\R)$, $g\in L^\infty(\R)$ with $\|f\|_1=2$, and $\|g\|_\infty=1$. Then \begin{align*} M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)=\sup_{\e>0}\frac{1}{2\e}\int\limits_{-\e}^\e |f(x-t)g(x-t^2)|dt\ge \frac{1}{2(|x|+1)}\int\limits_{-(|x|+1)}^{|x|+1}f(x-t)g(x-t^2)dt. \end{align*} Suppose $x>2$, then \begin{align*} M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)\ge \frac{1}{2(x+1)}\int\limits_{x-1}^{x+1}f(x-t)g(x-t^2)dt=\frac{1}{2(x+1)}\int\limits_{x-1}^{x+1}g(x-t^2)dt\gtrsim\frac{1}{x+1}. \end{align*} Therefore, $M_\Gamma(f,g)$ is not absolutely integrable.
nodes.statement_short: For the explicit pair with $\gamma(t)=t^2$, choosing $\e=|x|+1$ gives $M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)\gtrsim\frac{1}{x+1}$ for $x>2$, which is not integrable.
nodes.section: 5.3 Behavior on $\{A\}\cup\{B\}$: triples $p=r=1,\, q=\infty$ and $p=\infty,\, q=r=1$

nodes.name: Weak-type $(1,\infty)\to1$ bound at the vertex $A$
nodes.statement: Notice that if $f\in L^1$ and $g\in L^\infty$ we have by \eqref{1inf1} \begin{align*} \{x\in\R:M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)>\alpha\}\subseteq \Big\{x\in\R:Mf(x)>\frac{\alpha}{\|g\|_\infty}\Big\}, \end{align*} for any $\alpha>0$. Thus, from the classical theory, we get that for any $\alpha>0$ the following holds: \begin{align*} |\{x\in\R:M_\Gamma(f,g)(x)>\alpha\}|\lesssim \frac{1}{\alpha}\|f\|_1 \|g\|_\infty\:. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Although $L^1$ boundedness fails at $A$, the sublevel sets of $M_\Gamma(f,g)$ obey the weak-type estimate $\frac{1}{\alpha}\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty$.
nodes.section: 5.3 Behavior on $\{A\}\cup\{B\}$: triples $p=r=1,\, q=\infty$ and $p=\infty,\, q=r=1$

nodes.name: Unboundedness at the vertex $B$ ($p=\infty$, $q=r=1$)
nodes.statement: In this situation we deal with the vertex $B$, given by $p=\infty,\, q=r=1$. We will show that there are functions $f\in L^\infty(\R)$ and $g\in L^1(\R)$ such that $M_\Gamma(f,g)$ is not bounded on $L^1$ for, say, $\gamma(t)=t^2$.
nodes.statement_short: There exist $f\in L^\infty$ and $g\in L^1$ with $M_\Gamma(f,g)\notin L^1$ for $\gamma(t)=t^2$.
conclusions: We will show that there are functions $f\in L^\infty(\R)$ and $g\in L^1(\R)$ such that $M_\Gamma(f,g)$ is not bounded on $L^1$ for, say, $\gamma(t)=t^2$.
nodes.section: 5.3 Behavior on $\{A\}\cup\{B\}$: triples $p=r=1,\, q=\infty$ and $p=\infty,\, q=r=1$

nodes.name: Counterexample at the vertex $B$: $f\equiv1$, $g=\chi_{[-1,1]}$, $\gamma(t)=t^2$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be the constant function 1, and let $g=\chi_{[-1,1]}\in L^1(\R)$.
nodes.section: 5.3 Behavior on $\{A\}\cup\{B\}$: triples $p=r=1,\, q=\infty$ and $p=\infty,\, q=r=1$

nodes.name: Proof of the unboundedness at the vertex $B$
